strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarial training can preserve clean generalization while exhibiting a substantial robust generalization gap.

Partial signal learning combined with memorization of example-specific noise offers an interpretable candidate mechanism. Connecting representation complexity with training dynamics is a potentially useful contribution.
The capacity sweeps, synthetic feature trajectories, and input-flatness measurements provide complementary qualitative observations relevant to the proposed explanation.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. A balanced distribution supported on two well-separated points can satisfy Assumptions 4.1–4.3, including existence of a clean but nonrobust linear classifier. Once both points occur with nonvanishing frequency in the training sample, o(1) robust training error precludes an Ω(1) robust population error. A restriction on sample coverage or distributional concentration is missing. Furthermore, Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes only, so the proof's assertion that all training balls are disjoint does not follow. Appendix F.1 also incorrectly claims uniform approximation of a generally discontinuous construction by continuous ReLU networks.

The clean-generalization argument in Theorem E.12 contains essential unsupported steps. Cubic functions of Gaussian noise are generally not sub-Gaussian, contrary to the assertion used for the clean-test-error tail bound. Projections onto different filters also share the same noise and need not be independent. Additionally, V_i = Θ(1) does not establish the claimed Θ(1) norm of every filter's noise component. Consequently, the central o(1) clean-test-error conclusion is not established by the supplied proof.

The training theorem uses a different threat model from the CGRO definition. Definition 5.6 restricts perturbations to the signal direction and leaves noise patches unchanged, whereas Definition 3.4 measures robust training error over the full norm ball. Small training loss against the restricted adversary does not establish small robust training error against the full adversary. Protecting the memorized noise also materially limits the mechanism's applicability to standard adversarial training.

The experiments do not resolve these theoretical gaps. Section 6.2 uses δ = α = 10, violating the strict δ < α condition in Assumption 5.7 and permitting complete removal of the signal patch. This does not validate the theorem's stated regime. The capacity sweeps cannot distinguish representational limitations from optimization failure, and flatness measurements do not uniquely establish local-indicator memorization. PGD step counts, attack step sizes and restarts, and seed-to-seed variability are not reported, limiting confidence in the robust accuracies and reproducibility.

The interpretation and originality of the capacity result need sharper qualification. Theorem 4.7 is a worst-case existence result closely related to Li et al. (2022); it does not establish exponential complexity for the structured distribution analyzed in Section 5 or for the image datasets. An existential lower bound under weaker assumptions also does not, by itself, extend beyond the previously established linear-separable hard instances. Separately, the CGRO definition concerns an endpoint generalization gap, and the dynamics theorem does not demonstrate the late-training deterioration in robust test accuracy used to motivate robust overfitting.

The additional generalization bound in Theorem B.1 is also invalid as stated. A constant classifier can have zero input-loss gradient while its loss varies across labels. Its empirical loss then differs from population loss because of random class frequencies, although the proposed generalization correction is identically zero. The smooth-density assumption does not exclude this counterexample. These correctness problems affect the research conclusions and require substantial revision before acceptance.
